claims.text: W particles in the initial W–Cu material have native oxide layers that contribute to poor wettability.
The initial W–Cu material tends to exhibit phase separation, voids, and inhomogeneous thermal transport.
A thin Ni coating will be deposited on W particles by PVD before low-temperature sintering.
Applying a Ni wetting layer to W particles will enhance W–Cu interfacial bonding.
Applying a Ni wetting layer to W particles will reduce void formation in W–Cu composites.
The Ni coating acts as a wetting layer that improves contact between W and Cu.
Improved W–Cu wettability during sintering produces a more uniform, less defective interface.
A more uniform W–Cu interface reduces voids and improves thermal connectivity.
A more uniform W–Cu interface improves mechanical connectivity.
Ni-coated W–Cu will have higher thermal conductivity than otherwise comparable composites made without the Ni coating.
Ni-coated W–Cu will have greater mechanical durability, including higher fracture strength, than composites made without the Ni coating.
Ni-coated W–Cu will have lower defect density than composites made without the Ni coating.
Conventional spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying without precoating typically causes phase separation, void formation, and compromised thermal performance.
Surface oxides on powder particles can hinder densification and limit wettability.
Processing below the boiling point of Cu avoids Cu vaporization.
The Ni-coating intervention remains effective under irradiation conditions representative of fusion-reactor joints.
The long-term stability of the Ni wetting layer under irradiation has not been fully established.
